title: Who built Saudi Arabia’s ‘Stonehenge’ and why? ‘The men’ aren’t saying.
text:
Who built Saudi Arabia’s ‘Stonehenge’ and why? ‘The men’ aren’t saying.
Long ignored by Saudi Arabia, the ancient columns of Al-Rajajil are embraced as part of the area’s rich pre-Islamic history. But much remains unknown about the stones, and a visit to the site leaves one with more questions than answers.
At the edge of Saudi Arabia’s vast northern desert, they suddenly leap out from the ground, like the fingers of a stone giant reaching up through the sands.
The clusters of leaning stone pillars are estimated to predate the rise of ancient Egypt by a thousand years.
More than a roadside oddity 29 miles off the main highway heading into Jordan, with their original purpose lost in time, these carefully arranged stones are what’s widely referred to as Saudi Arabia’s Stonehenge.
Long ignored by Saudi Arabia, the ancient columns of Al-Rajajil are now embraced as part of the area’s rich pre-Islamic history. But much remains unknown about the stones, which from afar resemble men, and a visit to the site leaves one with more questions than answers.
While many of the Middle East’s archaeological sites invoke pharaohs, Nabataeans, Romans, Islamic civilization, and Crusaders, the columns of Al-Rajajil are an echo of a prehistoric period wrapped in mystery.
Saudi Arabia’s largely arid landscape is dotted by about a million prehistoric stone structures, but Al-Rajajil remains the most famous.
The columns stand at a strategic crossroads connecting the Red Sea, the Arabian Peninsula, and the Levant.
At the end of a road cutting between date farms south of the town of Sakaka, a gated 15-acre field emerges. There, 54 clusters of stone columns more than 6,000 years old point and fan out in every direction, like prehistoric missiles aimed at the sky.
The stone pillars were cut and shaped using a technique still unknown to researchers. Experts believe they were brought to the site from a faraway location, also unknown.
Judging by modern sensibilities and available research methods, there appears to be little rhyme or reason as to how these pillars are arranged.
Some columns are short and stout, while others are tall – the tallest is 13 feet. Some stand in a line; others are splayed out.
A few pillars are inscribed with the faint drawings of humans, four-legged animals of an unidentifiable species, and a series of mysterious symbols: circles, lines, and misshapen triangles.
But what, exactly, were they for?
The markings lead some experts to believe that the site had ceremonial purposes for the seminomadic herders known to have frequented the area thousands of years ago.
Alas, the columns were situated before the existence of written language, before their own stories could be etched in stone.
In recent centuries, local Arab tribes here in the Al Jouf region called the site Al-Rajajil – in Arabic, “the men” – because, from a distance, the weathered pillars resemble groups of people standing on the horizon.
It is not just a local legend. From afar in the haze of the desert sun, the columns almost look like narrow, distorted people, aliens standing in a distant vista.
The megalithic site is one of the more unusual sites in the Arab world, and dates to between the fifth and fourth millennium B.C., the late Neolithic or start of the Chalcolithic period, at the very beginning of the Copper Age.
The place that is now part of northern Saudi Arabia was a very different region back then.
These arid plains dotted with date palms were once full of natural lakes and lush pastures on which local inhabitants roamed and grazed their livestock.
Semisedentary groups, whether tribes or large family clans, would have traveled to chase pastures for grazing but are believed to have stayed within the same geographic region and would return to sites such as Al-Rajajil to live, trade, and bury their dead.
Archaeologists over the years have posed different theories as to the carefully grouped stone slabs’ purpose:
- Headstones for a collective burial ground
- An astronomical chart
- Markers demarcating tribal land
- An arena for social gatherings
- Or simply stone beacons guiding wary travelers along trade routes or signaling the existence of a settlement
Excavations over the past few decades have revealed tombs, pottery, serrated blades, arrowheads, human and animal bones, cairns, and a residential building with stairs – indicating that Al-Rajajil might have been a village.
But even the site’s plush and modern visitors center, where a staff of four offers dates and coffee, and presents a documentary on the region’s history, leaves visitors with more questions than answers.
Long ignored by Saudi Arabia, the columns of Al-Rajajil are now embraced by authorities as part of the area’s rich pre-Islamic history – a bid to encourage tourism to the kingdom’s remote regions and recognize the role of the prehistoric northern Arabian Peninsula in human development.
In 2023, the columns of Al-Rajajil were nominated, along with other stone megaliths in Saudi Arabia, to be added to the UNESCO World Heritage List, as the Prehistoric Stone Structures in Saudi Arabia.
In its petition adding Al-Rajajil to UNESCO’s tentative list of heritage sites, the Saudi government noted that it remains a “still largely unresearched heritage” and that “research in this field is still in its infancy.”
Yet the columns of Al-Rajajil remain a site well off the beaten path.
On a late morning in April, a Monitor correspondent was the first visitor in more than a week. For months, the Monitor repeatedly contacted the Saudi Heritage Commission for expert comment but did not receive a response.
One leaves the site with Al-Rajajil remaining a stranger.
“The men” still stand silently on the horizon, refusing to tell their story.
